BUYER GUIDE

From sample to shipment: approving cumin, fennel, sesame and alfalfa lots

Connect sample approval, test reports and shipment identity, with practical checks for spice buyers and alfalfa planting seed importers.

By Shiva Exim · Business contact: Savan Patel · 15 November 2026

A sample may look right while the shipment paperwork describes a different lot. Before loading cumin, fennel, sesame or alfalfa seed, make one final connection: does the material being packed match the sample, specification and evidence the buyer actually approved?

Key points

  • Record one consistent lot identity across samples, reports and shipment records.
  • Approve appearance and analytical results as separate decisions.
  • Check seed-test certificates by their scope, not just their colour.
  • Write down what is accepted and what still needs resolution before loading.

1. Give the approval an identity

Our recommended first step is an approval record naming the product, intended use, declared origin, crop year, lot number, quantity and sample reference. Record who drew the sample, when it was drawn and which packed or bulk lot it represents. Ask the supplier to explain how that identity will appear on the bags and shipment documents.

For example, approval of a fennel reference sample does not automatically approve a replacement lot. If the lot, processing stage or specification changes, ask which earlier tests and approvals still apply and what needs to be repeated. Keep a retained sample under agreed storage conditions for comparison if a question arises later.

2. Separate what you can see from what must be tested

Colour, seed size, visible foreign matter and aroma are useful sample checks. They do not establish every analytical result. Codex’s cumin standard, CXS 327-2017, amended in 2021 and 2022, addresses physical and chemical characteristics, hygiene and lot acceptance separately. It provides a technical reference for cumin; it should not be silently applied as a fennel or sesame standard.

For cumin and fennel, Shiva Exim’s 99% Europe and 99% Singapore descriptions are commercial quality labels. Agree what purity measures, the test method and the other acceptance limits. Neither label is certification or blanket approval for a destination.

For sesame, confirm natural or hulled form before assessing colour, defects and the relevant food-quality tests. A visibly clean sample does not replace microbiological or residue evidence.

3. Read the report against the order

As a procurement check, compare the laboratory name, report number, sample and lot references, sampling and test dates, methods, units, results and agreed limits. A certificate of analysis should be read for the parameters it actually covers. A generic statement such as “tested” does not tell the buyer which substances or organisms were examined, or at what reporting limits.

Agree the required test panel and sampling arrangements before commissioning work. For EU-bound food, the European Commission’s pesticides database helps identify product-specific maximum residue levels; the Commission states that the database is informational and official legal information is published in the EU Official Journal. This guide sets no numerical residue limits and makes no destination compliance determination. The importer should confirm applicable requirements for the specific product and shipment.

4. Use the same questions across origins

Origin is part of traceability, not an automatic quality ranking. The following comparison set reflects Shiva Exim’s buying interests; it is not a claim that these are the only producing countries or that Shiva Exim currently offers every origin.

Product and originsEvidence to request for the offered lot
Sesame — India, Brazil, PakistanDeclared origin and crop season; natural or hulled form; sample identity; agreed colour, purity and defect criteria; buyer-required microbiological and contaminant reports.
Cumin — India, Egypt, ChinaOrigin, crop year and lot; whole or other agreed form; cleaning and physical-quality limits; moisture and aroma-related requirements; required analytical panel.
Fennel — India, EgyptOrigin, crop year and lot; agreed colour and size reference; purity and moisture criteria; aroma and buyer-required tests.

Ask the same core questions when changing origin or supplier. Do not assume an earlier sample approval or test report transfers to the next consignment. This article supplies no new national crop estimate or available-stock figure for these origins.

5. Alfalfa planting seed needs a separate evidence check

Alfalfa seed in Shiva Exim’s portfolio is for agricultural planting to establish a fodder crop. Specify the actual variety requirement, growing destination, treatment or coating status, physical purity, normal germination, hard-seed reporting, other-seed content and test date. The commercial single-year and multi-year labels are not guarantees of stand life or yield.

ISTA’s official FAQ explains that a Blue International Seed Sample Certificate concerns the submitted sample at receipt; seed lot certificates concern the lot at sampling. Buyers should therefore check the scope of the certificate requested and supplied. ISTA’s current rules page identifies its 2026 edition, including certificate and sampling chapters.

OECD Seed Schemes concern varietal certification under harmonised official procedures. That is a different purpose from reporting seed-test results. Specify the exact certificate, label and variety evidence your buyer requires, and confirm applicability and availability before committing. This guide does not claim that Shiva Exim holds an ISTA certificate or OECD certification for an offered lot.

6. Make the loading decision explicit

Our suggested release record has five fields: lot and quantity; approved sample reference; agreed specification; accepted report/document references; and the person and date authorising release. Record any exceptions separately. An unresolved identity mismatch or missing agreed test should be clarified before that lot is released.

Before loading, compare the lot marks, packing list and actual packed material against that record. Agree how a proposed substitution or repacking will be handled. This is an operational recommendation, not a claim that testing eliminates all shipment risk.

Keep crop outlook separate from lot approval

Shiva Exim’s view, first supplied on 12 October 2026, is that weaker rainfall in Gujarat and Rajasthan may reduce Indian cumin, fennel and sesame production in 2027. That remains a provisional opinion, pending district rainfall, irrigation, acreage, harvest and carryover evidence. It does not establish the quality or availability of a particular lot, and this buyer guide does not update that forecast or predict prices.

Sources

Checked 15 November 2026. Dates below identify the standard or edition; undated pages are labelled as such.

  • FAO/WHO Codex: Standard for Cumin, CXS 327-2017 — adopted 2017; amended 2021 and 2022. Technical reference for cumin characteristics and lot acceptance.
  • European Commission: EU Pesticides Database — undated live information page. Explains product/residue searches and the authority of Official Journal texts.
  • ISTA: Accreditation FAQs, question 4 — undated. Explains sample-certificate and lot-certificate scope.
  • ISTA: International Rules for Seed Testing — 2026 edition listed. Sampling, testing and reporting framework.
  • OECD: Seed Schemes — undated overview; lists a varieties download updated July 2026. Explains varietal certification.
  • Shiva Exim’s company-confirmed cumin, fennel, sesame and alfalfa product guides — reviewed in the linked Site’s current source on 15 November 2026.

Lot availability, testing, documentation and terms require confirmation for each enquiry. Market estimates may change. Shiva Exim’s 2027 outlook is provisional.
